definition: A huge group of many billions of stars, held together by gravity. The Sun is one star in our galaxy, the Milky Way.
The galaxy that contains the Sun and the Solar System. It is made up of many billions of stars and is about 100 000 light-years across.
A unit of distance, not time: the distance light travels through the vacuum of space in one year. One light-year is about $9.5 \times 10^{15}$ m.
An interstellar cloud of gas and dust that is collapsing under its own gravitational attraction and getting hotter as it does so. It is the stage before a stable star.

The large red star that a less massive star, such as the Sun, expands into when most of the hydrogen in its centre has become helium. It later forms a planetary nebula with a white dwarf at its centre.
The very large star that a much more massive star expands into when most of the hydrogen in its centre has become helium. It later explodes as a supernova.
A small, hot, very dense star left at the centre of a planetary nebula, at the end of the life of a less massive star such as the Sun.

The huge explosion of a red supergiant at the end of a massive star's life. It throws out a nebula of hydrogen and newly made heavier elements, and leaves a neutron star or a black hole at its centre.
A small, extremely dense star that can be left at the centre after a supernova.
An object so dense that nothing can escape its gravity, not even light. One can be left at the centre after a supernova.
A glowing shell of gas thrown off by a red giant, with a white dwarf at its centre. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets.
A huge cloud of gas and dust in space. The nebula from a supernova holds hydrogen and newly made heavier elements, and may later form new stars with planets.
